endorsements.title: CHAI Responsible AI Guide (Assurance Standards Guide)
endorsements.quote: Deploy the AI system in a local, simulated environment • Assess system performance, potential impact and generalizability

endorsements.title: Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Device Software Functions: Lifecycle Management and Marketing Submission Recommendations (draft guidance)
endorsements.quote: Specifically, as part of design controls, a manufacturer must “establish and maintain procedures for validating the device design,” which “shall ensure that devices conform to defined user needs and intended uses and shall include testing of production units under actual or simulated use conditions”

endorsements.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1)
endorsements.issuer: National Institute of Standards and Technology
endorsements.quote: Organizations should follow applicable human subjects research requirements, and best practices such as informed consent and subject compensation, when implementing feedback activities.

endorsements.title: Considerations for the regulation of generative AI-enabled medical devices (discussion paper)
endorsements.quote: CDRH is therefore considering that clinical confirmation may be a necessary step in addition to benchmarking to determine whether a GenAI-enabled device performs as intended for its intended population under real-world or clinically representative conditions.

endorsements.title: Consensus-Based Minimum Requirements for the Adoption of a Computational Pathology Algorithm for Tumor Budding in Colorectal Cancer: An Early Health Technology Assessment
endorsements.quote: To evaluate whether the CPath TB algorithm meets requirements such as compatibility, flexibility, and usability in a specific setting, pathology laboratories could use a structured validation process, as described in the review by van der Laak et al.

evidence.title: Does LLM Assistance Improve Healthcare Delivery? An Evaluation Using On-site Physicians and Laboratory Tests∗
evidence.outcome: Agreement between chart-based retrospective review and on-site real-world clinical evaluation of LLM-assisted plans
evidence.effect: Retrospective academic reviewers rated LLM-assisted plans more favorably, while on-site physicians and laboratory tests showed little to no improvement, revealing a gap between chart review and real-world relevance.
evidence.quote: This highlights a gap between chart-based reviews and real-world clinical relevance that may be especially important in evaluating the effectiveness of LLM-based interventions.

evidence.title: Comparison of humans versus mobile phone-powered artificial intelligence for the diagnosis and management of pigmented skin cancer in secondary care: a multicentre, prospective, diagnostic, clinical trial
evidence.outcome: Real-world clinical accuracy of AI versus experimental (online reader study) performance
evidence.effect: The ISIC AI algorithm, superior in experimental studies, was significantly inferior to specialists in the clinic (-11·6% [-20·3 to -3·0]) for diagnosis.
evidence.quote: An AI algorithm that was superior in experimental studies was significantly inferior to specialists in a real-world scenario, suggesting that caution is needed when extrapolating results of experimental studies to clinical practice.
evidence.sample_unit: suspicious pigmented lesions (diagnostic trial; 124 patients); management trial 5696 lesions from 66 patients

evidence.title: Early stroke diagnosis and evaluation based on pathological voice classification using speech enhancement
evidence.outcome: Real-time stroke voice system accuracy in clinical trial and WeChat mini-program tests versus offline results
evidence.effect: Among 34 subjects, sustained vowels achieved 85.29% accuracy (four patients misclassified, one undetermined); two-stage strategy (SVs then SS) achieved 100% overall accuracy.
evidence.quote: Results demonstrated that among 34 subjects (24 patients and 10 healthy individuals), SVs achieved 85.29 % accuracy, with four patients misclassified and one patient undetermined.

evidence.title: Effectiveness of artificial intelligence-based diabetic retinopathy screening in primary care and endocrinology settings in Australia: a pragmatic trial
evidence.outcome: AI performance in real-world clinic use conditions across five sites
evidence.effect: In real-world primary care and endocrinology clinics, AI achieved 93.3% accuracy, with 86% of patients and 85% of care providers highly satisfied.
evidence.quote: The AI-assisted DR screening model was accurate and well received by patients and staff in Australian primary care and endocrinology clinics.

evidence.title: A Principle-based Framework for the Development and Evaluation of Large Language Models for Health and Wellness
evidence.outcome: Whether real-world user feedback adds to isolated technical evaluations
evidence.effect: Real-world feedback led to targeted improvements and showed the need to combine isolated technical evaluations with real-world user feedback; no numeric results reported.
evidence.quote: This process guided targeted improvements to the system and demonstrated the necessity of combining isolated technical evaluations with real-world user feedback.

evidence.title: Diabetic Retinopathy Screening Using Smartphone-Based Fundus Photography and Deep-Learning Artificial Intelligence in the Yucatan Peninsula: A Field Study
evidence.venue: Journal of diabetes science and technology
evidence.outcome: AI DR detection performance in real-world remote field setting
evidence.effect: Medios sensitivity 94% (88%-97%) and specificity 94% (88%-98%); EyeArt sensitivity 94% and specificity 86% in field setting.
evidence.quote: Medios and EyeArt AI algorithms demonstrated high levels of sensitivity and specificity for detecting DR when applied in this real-world field setting.

evidence.title: Clinical Validation of Computer-Aided Diagnosis Software for Preventing Retained Surgical Sponges
evidence.venue: Journal of the American College of Surgeons
evidence.outcome: Specificity of CAD in clinical setting versus development-phase performance
evidence.effect: CAD flagged possible retained items in 150 of 1,053 images; specificity 85.8%, similar to development-phase data, so real-world performance matched development performance.
evidence.quote: Specificity was 85.8%, which is similar to the data obtained during the development of the software.

evidence.title: Large-scale observational study of AI-based patient and surgical material verification system in ophthalmology: real-world evaluation in 37 529 cases
evidence.outcome: system accuracy in pre-implementation testing
evidence.effect: The system demonstrated 100% accuracy in a pre-implementation test of 300 cases.
evidence.quote: Pre-implementation testing with 300 cases (50% intentionally erroneous) demonstrated 100% system accuracy ( online supplemental figure 6 ).

evidence.title: EvoApneaFormer: an IoT and prognostic evolutionary deep learning-based framework for real-time multi-event sleep apnea disorder detection and remote monitoring
evidence.outcome: Model performance in real-world clinical and home settings, including under signal artifacts
evidence.effect: Accuracy 99.8% in clinical and 96.9% in home settings, robust to motion artifacts and signal dropouts.
evidence.quote: Real-world trials confirmed robustness in both clinical 99.8% and home 96.9% settings, even under motion artifacts and signal dropouts.

evidence.title: Large Language Model Performance in UK Advice & Guidance: A Pilot Study in Neurology
evidence.outcome: LLM performance on real-world Advice & Guidance cases versus specialist responses
evidence.effect: Aggregate scores similar (outcome 84% vs 82%, p=0.67; safety 3.98 vs 4.02), but 10% of LLM responses had concerning scores vs 0% human.
evidence.quote: Although there were no statistically significant differences between blinded specialist neurologists and LLM responses across any domain (outcome: 84% vs 82%, p=0.67; safety: 3.98 vs 4.02, p=0.85; efficacy: 4.06 vs 3.98, p=0.61; feasibility: 4.39 vs 4.20, p=0.45), 10% of LLM responses received concerning scores (≤2 average score) compared to 0% of human responses, indicating potentially clinically important tail risk.

evidence.title: Standardised evaluation and monitoring of site-specific AI performance with physical CT phantoms
evidence.outcome: site-specific testing
evidence.effect: Clinically realistic phantoms provided a feasible method for standardized, site-specific testing of AI under simulated local acquisition conditions.
evidence.quote: Our findings show that clinically realistic phantoms enable standardised, site-specific testing and monitoring of AI, providing a proactive method for local and cross-institutional quality assurance.

evidence.title: LUMANA: A Scenario-Based Field Validation of a Culturally Adapted AI System for Mental Health Screening in Sokoto State, Nigeria
evidence.outcome: Performance under simulated local use conditions via scenario-based field validation
evidence.effect: Scenario-based field validation in Sokoto found outputs largely acceptable and identified three improvements needed before pilot.
evidence.quote: Three operational improvements were identified before pilot implementation: clearer protocols for interpreting distress, refinement of language to minimise potentially stigmatizing expressions, and automatic escalation of suspected psychotic symptoms.
evidence.sample_unit: stakeholders completing structured evaluations (136 AI output safety assessments across 8 scenarios)

evidence.title: Mind the gap: emergent clinical risk at the interface of two individually safe AI systems in a multilingual ambient scribe
evidence.outcome: Whether component-level performance predicts end-to-end note risk
evidence.effect: Low serious-error rates in individual layers (3.4% intrinsic) did not preclude higher end-to-end note risk (up to 24% at L4/L5); component-level metrics could not fully capture risk.
evidence.quote: Low serious-error rates in individual layers did not preclude higher end-to-end note risk.
evidence.sample_unit: scripted consultation sessions (end-to-end arm; 385 in intrinsic arm)
languages: 77 languages including high-, medium-, and low-resource languages

evidence.title: Assessing The Performance of Multimodal Large Language Models in Diagnosing and Staging Diabetic Retinopathy: An External Validation Study of Large Language Models
evidence.outcome: Multimodal LLM sensitivity for DR detection, referable DR, DR staging, and maculopathy on local hospital fundus images
evidence.effect: GPT-4 sensitivity 82% for DR and 80% for referable DR, meeting UK NICE criteria; all LLMs performed poorly in DR staging and diabetic maculopathy detection.
evidence.quote: However, all LLMs, including GPT-4, performed poorly in staging DR and detecting diabetic maculopathy.

evidence.title: Brain tumour segmentation with incomplete imaging data
evidence.outcome: Segmentation accuracy on heterogeneous real-world local clinical imaging sample
evidence.effect: On a 50-patient real-world tertiary-centre sample spanning 15 years, accuracy was maintained on non-isotropic acquisitions and post-operative imaging with tumour recurrence.
evidence.quote: Our analysis includes validation on a heterogeneous, real-world 50 patient sample of brain tumour imaging acquired over the last 15 years at our tertiary centre, demonstrating maintained accuracy even on non-isotropic MRI acquisitions, or even on complex post-operative imaging with tumour recurrence.

evidence.title: Real world deployment of a pancreatic cancer risk model: impact of refitting, imputation, and computational burden
evidence.outcome: Runtime in simulated deployment
evidence.effect: Simulation identified scalability differences: SMI 383.77 min/batch; IFCE 19.54 min/batch while capturing 22.91% of top-2.5% cases.
evidence.quote: In contrast, SMI was not only less effective in prediction but also computationally intensive, requiring an average of over 6 h per batch (383.77 min), which may limit scalability.

evidence.title: Simulated evaluation of large language model stepwise diagnostic reasoning with real-world chest pain encounters and Bayesian networks
evidence.venue: BMC medical informatics and decision making
evidence.outcome: LLM diagnostic performance in stepwise simulation with real ED data versus static vignette expectations
evidence.effect: In simulated stepwise setting with real data, GPT-4o over-predicted rare conditions (sensitivity 79.3%, specificity 45.2%) and diverged from physicians and BN-optimal pathways (RBO 0.060-0.097).
evidence.quote: The relatively low diagnostic accuracy we observed may partly reflect this closer adherence to real-world complexity.

evidence.title: Error Detection in Emergency Radiology Reports Using a Large Language Model: Multistage Evaluation Study
evidence.outcome: Real-world validation of LLM error detection on verified reports
evidence.effect: In real-world validation on 800 reports, DeepSeek-R1 identified 117 true reporting errors, positive predictive value 56.5%.
evidence.quote: In real-world validation, DeepSeek-R1 identified 117 true reporting errors, yielding a positive predictive value of 56.5%.
evidence.sample_unit: emergency radiology reports (dataset 1); 200 reports stage 1, 100 stages 2-3, 800 stage 4

evidence.title: Continuous prediction and clinical alarm management of late-onset sepsis in preterm infants using vital signs from a patient monitor
evidence.venue: Computer methods and programs in biomedicine
evidence.outcome: simulated real-time alarm performance
evidence.effect: 24 h multi-threshold policy: sensitivity 71.6 %, PPV 9.9 %, average 1.15 alarms per day per patient.
evidence.quote: When setting the expected alarm window to 24 h and using a multi-threshold alarm policy, the sensitivity metric was 71.6 %, while the positive predictive value was 9.9 %, resulting in an average of 1.15 alarms per day per patient.

evidence.title: Schema Enforcement and Structured-Output Stability in Locally Deployed LLMs for Clinical Admission-Note Editing: A Proxy-Based Pre-Deployment Evaluation
evidence.outcome: Model behavior under local deployment conditions and chat-template constraints versus expectations
evidence.effect: Same-size models differed substantially in structured-output stability under the identical local environment; embedded system instructions increased failures (persistent failure 5.0% vs 0.3%).
evidence.quote: In this study, all three models were similar in size and were evaluated under the same local environment, yet their structured-output stability and documentation behavior differed substantially.

evidence.title: Intelligent Framework for Adverse Drug Event Identification Using Large Language Models and Retrieval-Augmented Generation: Development and Evaluation Study
evidence.outcome: Performance on uncurated real-world notes with ~4.6% ADE prevalence versus curated balanced set
evidence.effect: Real-world DeepSeek-V3 RAG L3 F1 0.8159 vs SAG 0.8134 (marginal), precision 0.7185, recall 0.9448, specificity 0.9821; NAG F1 0.6380.
evidence.quote: At the L3 level, RAG achieved an F 1 -score of 0.8159 (95% CI 0.7736‐0.8598), compared with 0.6380 (95% CI 0.5759‐0.6942) for NAG and 0.8134 (95% CI 0.7600‐0.8627) for SAG.

evidence.title: Triaging mammography with artificial intelligence: an implementation study
evidence.outcome: Real-world prioritization rate vs retrospective expectation
evidence.effect: AI prioritized 29% of cases in deployment vs 14% anticipated from retrospective testing, requiring more immediate reads than planned.
evidence.quote: First, the proportion of cases prioritized by AI for immediate radiologist review was 29%, much higher than the proportion anticipated based on retrospective testing (14%).

evidence.title: Prospective Real-Time Validation of a Lung Ultrasound Deep Learning Model in the ICU
evidence.outcome: Translation of previously validated classification performance to real-time bedside use
evidence.effect: Bedside performance was reported as equally good as prior validation: accuracy of 95%, sensitivity of 93%, and specificity of 96% against expert annotation.
evidence.quote: A previously validated DL classification model performs equally well in real-time at the bedside when platformed on a portable device.

evidence.title: Implementation of deep learning artificial intelligence in vision-threatening disease screenings for an underserved community during COVID-19
evidence.outcome: AI referral accuracy and ungradable rate in real-world community non-mydriatic screenings versus gold standard
evidence.effect: 38.9% of eyes ungradable by AI versus 2.6% by humans; sensitivity 63.2%, specificity 94.5%, PPV 32.0%, NPV 98.4%; all 4 eyes with multiple diseases referred.
evidence.quote: Deep learning artificial intelligence had 63.2% sensitivity, 94.5% specificity, 32.0% positive predictive value, and 98.4% negative predictive value in vision-threatening disease referrals.

evidence.title: Comparison of the use of a clinically implemented deep learning segmentation model with the simulated study setting for breast cancer patients receiving radiotherapy

evidence.quote: Ninety-three percent of all contours in clinic were scored as clinically acceptable or usable as a starting point, comparable to 92% achieved in the pilot study.

evidence.title: Real-World Evaluation of AI-Driven Diabetic Retinopathy Screening in Public Health Settings: Validation and Implementation Study

evidence.effect: Sensitivity rose from 68.4% to 99.6% while specificity fell from 96% to 64.7%; DME sensitivity only 26.5%.
evidence.quote: The AI-3 algorithm’s sensitivity increased significantly from 68.4% to 99.6%, while specificity decreased from 96% to 64.7% between the validation and implementation phases.

evidence.title: Tele-ophthalmology-enabled and artificial intelligence-ready referral pathway for community optometry referrals of retinal disease: HERMES cluster randomised trial with a diagnostic accuracy study
evidence.outcome: AI processing rate and referral accuracy in real-world optometry settings
evidence.effect: Octane processed images from only 204 of 396 participants (51.5%); could not process 48.5%; generalisability challenges in real-world evaluation.
evidence.quote: The artificial intelligence model presented challenges relating to its generalisability in a real-world evaluation context.

evidence.title: Artificial intelligence-based smartphone application for skin cancer detection: a prospective diagnostic accuracy study

evidence.quote: Image capture was unsuccessful in 16.6% of lesions (n = 317/1904), despite optimal conditions.

evidence.title: ArcMAP - ML assisted medical concept mapping to accelerate NHS data standardization
evidence.outcome: Real-world lab test mapping accuracy vs published benchmark performance
evidence.effect: Models reporting 80%-90% top-1 on standard benchmarks achieved baseline top-1 below 40% on real NHS laboratory test names (BioLORD 37.0%).
evidence.quote: Consequently, baseline top-1 accuracies remain below 40%, underscoring that pre-training on biomedical literature and ontology definitions alone is insufficient to capture the extreme variability and abbreviation patterns encountered in laboratory test naming.

evidence.title: CATalyze-AI: accelerating referral for thrombectomy in acute stroke patients using an AI-based software. A prospective, multicentre, quasi-experimental cohort study

evidence.title: When Digital Health Falls Short: Limited Validity of an AI-Powered App for Dietary Assessment in Females with Obesity

evidence.effect: SNAQ underestimated energy intake by 25% (2187 ± 1401 vs 3004 ± 481 kcal/day; p = 0.01). Limits of agreement were -3707 to 2073 kcal/day and within-subject ICC was 0.00.

evidence.title: Performance of AI-based diabetic retinopathy screening is highly dependent on evaluation setting: A five-year, multi-framework study

evidence.effect: Substantial variability in sensitivity and specificity across the VA, Finland, and NHS evaluations, despite near-perfect benchmark performance on Messidor-2.
evidence.quote: Across these evaluation frameworks, substantial variability in observed sensitivity and specificity was found.

evidence.title: Feasibility study of an AI-powered mobile app to support cutaneous leishmaniasis diagnosis in the Brazilian Amazon

evidence.title: A Real-World Evaluation of LLM Medication Safety Reviews in NHS Primary Care

evidence.effect: Mean imputation and execution time per batch: SME 0.71 min, IFCE 19.54 min, SMI 383.77 min; data extraction 13.30 hours.

evidence.title: Opportunities and Challenges of Visual Large Language Models in Imaging Diagnostics: Lessons from Brain Metastasis Detection in Clinical MRI

evidence.title: Comparative evaluation of multimodal large language models for diagnostic accuracy in pediatric electrocardiography: a prospective comparative diagnostic accuracy study

evidence.title: Stop Listening to Me! How Multi-turn Conversations Can Degrade LLM Reliability

evidence.title: Active Evidence-Seeking and Diagnostic Reasoning in Large Language Models for Clinical Decision Support

evidence.title: Evaluating large language models for clinical note processing: local fine-tuning and internal-external validation using electronic health records from South Asia

commentary.bottom_line: Twenty-one studies suggest that local or simulated testing often reveals performance gaps that benchmarks miss; for example, a skin-lesion algorithm that outperformed specialists in experimental reader studies scored 11.6% lower than specialists in clinic. No study compares deployments that did and did not undergo local testing, so the evidence shows that the practice detects problems but not that it prevents patient harm.

perspectives.view: Four of 21 studies are prospective comparisons in real deployment, and the rest use descriptive, replay, or benchmark designs. Most studies measure whether local testing detected a gap, not whether testing changed patient outcomes. Indirectness and inconsistency, including four null or mixed results, lead me to rate certainty as low.

Low serious-error rates in single components (3.4%) coexisted with end-to-end note risk of up to 24%. In a stepwise simulation, GPT-4o reached 45.2% specificity, and 10% of LLM advice responses had concerning safety scores compared with 0% of specialist responses. These findings suggest that system-level local testing may catch failure modes before they reach patients.

Local configuration changed model behavior. Embedded system instructions raised persistent structured-output failure from 0.3% to 5.0% in the same environment. A simulated deployment found batch runtimes from 19.54 to 383.77 minutes, and scenario-based validation in Sokoto identified three fixes before pilot. Phantom-based testing appeared feasible for site-specific imaging checks.

A field test in rural Mexico reported 94% sensitivity for two retinal screening tools. In hazard studies, an Indian safety-net site saw specificity fall from 96% to 64.7%, and U.S. community screenings found 38.9% of eyes ungradable by AI compared with 2.6% by humans. These results suggest that performance may shift in lower-resource settings.

FDA design controls already require device testing under actual or simulated use conditions, and CDRH is considering clinical confirmation beyond benchmarking for generative AI devices. One simulated test against prespecified criteria found that a locked triage configuration failed its undertriage criteria. This finding suggests how deployer-side testing could apply the same logic before go-live.

In one trial, AI prioritized 29% of cases in deployment against 14% expected from retrospective testing, which increased immediate reads. In one simulated pipeline, data extraction took 13.30 hours. One site ran a 300-case pre-implementation test in a program covering 37,529 surgeries. These figures suggest that local testing carries staff time costs but may prevent workload surprises.

In one five-site clinic study, 86% of patients reported being highly satisfied under real-world use. Feedback from 13,000 consented users led to targeted improvements. NIST advises informed consent and compensation when people take part in feedback activities, which bears on trust when local testing involves real patients.

commentary.research_gap: No study compares sites that performed pre-deployment local testing with sites that did not. None reports whether problems found in testing were corrected and whether patient outcomes then changed. Studies also offer no standard for local test sample size or for performance thresholds that should halt go-live.
commentary.underserved_note: Several tests of the practice included non-English-speaking populations, including in China and Nigeria, and one included rural and disabled patients in Mexico. No test enrolled Medicaid, U.S. safety-net, or low-literacy populations. The only safety-net study is a hazard study from India, which found specificity falling from 96% to 64.7% at an implementation site. This result suggests that local testing may matter in settings where direct evidence is sparse.
